questions.question: What best describes artificial intelligence?
options: Only systems that learn from labeled examples
Only multilayer neural-network systems
Computer systems performing tasks associated with intelligence
Only systems that generate new language
questions.explanation: AI includes recognition, prediction, language processing and other computational tasks.

questions.question: Which event is associated with the formal founding of AI?
options: The 1986 connectionism books
The 1997 Deep Blue match
The 2012 ImageNet competition
The 1956 Dartmouth workshop
questions.explanation: The notes associate the field's founding with Dartmouth and John McCarthy.

questions.question: What distinguishes symbolic AI?
options: Explicit human-written rules and symbols
Weights adjusted from labeled examples
Categories discovered in unlabeled data
Action values updated from rewards
questions.explanation: Symbolic systems make rules inspectable, but depend on anticipating relevant situations.

questions.question: Why can a symbolic clinical tool be brittle?
options: Its rules automatically adapt to every unseen case
Its rules may not cover unfamiliar situations
Its transparency prevents any clinical error
Its rules are learned without human knowledge
questions.explanation: Rules work within the situations their designers anticipated.

questions.question: How is knowledge typically represented in subsymbolic AI?
options: Explicit rules elicited from clinicians
A readable chain of logical propositions
Numerical weights learned from examples
A manually written list of category definitions
questions.explanation: Learned knowledge is distributed across numerical parameters and can be difficult to explain.

questions.question: An expert labels recordings typical or disordered. Which learning approach uses these examples?
options: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Manual rule execution only
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses examples with target labels.

questions.question: A system groups children by similar performance without diagnostic labels. This is what type of learning?
options: Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised learning
Backward chaining
questions.explanation: Unsupervised methods discover structure in unlabeled data.

questions.question: A system improves actions through rewards. Which learning approach is this?
options: Reinforcement learning
Rule-based inference
Static transcription
Supervised classification
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning uses feedback on actions rather than correct labels for every example.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a training set?
options: To learn model parameters
To produce an independent final performance estimate
To confirm performance after deployment only
To select the best score after repeated test submissions
questions.explanation: Training examples are used during learning.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a held-out test set?
options: To select weights through repeated feedback
To replace the need for a training set
To assess performance on unseen examples
To establish that a model understands every case
questions.explanation: A test set estimates generalization only when it remains independent of model development.

questions.question: Why does repeatedly adjusting a model to improve its test score undermine evaluation?
options: It converts supervised learning into reinforcement learning
It removes any need for external validation
It makes the test set more representative automatically
The test set begins influencing development
questions.explanation: Repeated test-driven tweaking makes the final score less independent.

questions.question: What does a simple perceptron do?
options: Selects the largest raw input without weighting
Thresholds a weighted sum of inputs
Predicts a word by matching it to a dictionary definition
Updates every input to the same numerical value
questions.explanation: A perceptron combines weighted inputs and compares the total with a threshold.

questions.question: Which sequence describes a layered neural network?
options: Input, output, hidden layers
Hidden layers, input, output
Input, hidden layers, output
Input, training labels, hidden layers only
questions.explanation: Hidden layers transform representations between input and output.

questions.question: How do the notes define a deep network?
options: A network with exactly one hidden layer
Any network trained on a large dataset
A network with more than one hidden layer
Any network with several output categories
questions.explanation: Depth refers to layered computational processing, not file size.

questions.question: What does back-propagation use to guide weight updates?
options: Error at the network output
Only the number of layers chosen by the designer
Only the predicted category without its error
Only the input signal before any comparison
questions.explanation: Error information is propagated backward through the network.

questions.question: What is an activation map in a ConvNet?
options: A list of final category predictions for every patient
The table of training and test labels
A grid of responses to a visual feature
The sequence of all weight updates over training
questions.explanation: ConvNets use feature detectors with shared weights across locations.

questions.question: Which is an example of natural language processing?
options: Translating or summarizing language
Classifying a voice sample using jitter alone
Detecting an object in a photograph
Learning a robot's movement from rewards
questions.explanation: NLP deals computationally with human language.

questions.question: What distinguishes generative AI?
options: It creates new content
It produces only predefined category labels
It only retrieves unchanged records from storage
It guarantees that generated content is factual
questions.explanation: Generative systems can create text, images, speech or other outputs.

questions.question: How does the notes' simplified account describe an LLM generating text?
options: Selecting only independently verified factual statements
Applying a fixed clinical rule to every case
Predicting likely next pieces of language
Retrieving a complete answer unchanged from one source
questions.explanation: Predicting plausible continuations does not guarantee truth.

questions.question: What does generalization mean?
options: Matching training examples with minimal error
Performing well on new unseen data
Choosing settings that maximize a test score after repeated tuning
Producing a clear explanation for every prediction
questions.explanation: Generalization concerns performance beyond the examples used for training.

questions.question: Which sequence represents a typical clinical AI pipeline?
options: Input data, feature extraction, prediction
Prediction, feature extraction, input data
Feature extraction, final diagnosis, consent
Training labels, care plan, input data
questions.explanation: Clinical AI transforms data into features and outputs that require interpretation.

questions.question: What is accuracy?
options: The proportion of flagged cases truly affected
The proportion of affected cases detected
The proportion of unaffected cases cleared
The proportion of all cases classified correctly
questions.explanation: Accuracy summarizes correct classifications across the evaluated sample.

questions.question: What is sensitivity also called?
options: Precision
Recall
Prompt dependence
Specificity
questions.explanation: Sensitivity measures how many genuinely affected cases are detected.

questions.question: What does specificity measure?
options: The proportion of unaffected cases correctly cleared
The total number of training examples
The proportion of affected cases detected
The proportion of positive predictions that are correct
questions.explanation: Specificity concerns true negatives among people without the difficulty.

questions.question: What does precision measure?
options: How many affected cases are detected
How many features are extracted
How many flagged cases truly have the difficulty
How many unaffected cases are cleared
questions.explanation: Precision uses flagged cases as its denominator.

questions.question: What does AUC broadly describe in the notes?
options: The proportion of flagged cases truly affected
Overall separation between two groups
The percentage of model predictions made with confidence
The proportion of unaffected cases correctly cleared at one threshold
questions.explanation: AUC summarizes discrimination; it does not establish clinical usefulness by itself.

questions.question: Why prioritize sensitivity in an early screening tool?
options: To maximize specificity even if more children are missed
To remove the need for follow-up assessment
To reduce missed children needing assessment
To guarantee that every flagged child has the difficulty
questions.explanation: Missing an affected child can delay access to early support.

questions.question: What should follow a positive screening result?
options: A final diagnosis based solely on the model score
A full clinical assessment
Immediate service eligibility based only on the flag
A repeat screen used as the only diagnostic evidence
questions.explanation: Screening flags risk and does not replace comprehensive assessment.

questions.question: What did the DLD example in the notes involve?
options: Only English-speaking adults
Cypriot Greek children
Only people with Parkinson's disease
Only written legal documents
questions.explanation: The example demonstrates that evidence is tied to a particular population.

questions.question: Which features mattered more in the cited DLD example?
options: Perception features
Demographic features alone
Production features
Caregiver-report features alone
questions.explanation: This is a study-specific result reported in the lecture notes, not a universal rule.

questions.question: The notes report about 75% accuracy for an autism-related model using what input?
options: Only acoustic measures such as jitter and shimmer
Only receptive-language test scores
Transcript features such as mean length of utterance
Only demographic and appointment data
questions.explanation: The reported result is tied to the example study and its dataset.

questions.question: Why may ordinary ASR perform poorly on disordered speech?
options: ASR is designed to classify diagnoses rather than transcribe speech
Disordered speech always has less background noise
More training data from typical adults necessarily fixes the mismatch
Its training data may underrepresent that speech
questions.explanation: Training examples influence which speech patterns a recognizer handles well.

questions.question: What improved ASR in the notes' example?
options: Testing repeatedly on the same conversational samples
Increasing the amount of typical adult speech only
Removing disordered examples to standardize the dataset
Adding conversational disordered-speech samples to training
questions.explanation: Relevant training examples can improve recognition for an underrepresented population.

questions.question: Which set contains voice acoustic measures listed in the notes?
options: Jitter, shimmer, spectral tilt and harmonic-to-noise ratio
Mean length of utterance, vocabulary diversity, syntax and semantics
Sensitivity, specificity, precision and AUC
Independent accuracy, supported accuracy, prompt dependence and NR
questions.explanation: These measures describe aspects of the voice signal.

questions.question: The notes report 88% classification accuracy for which comparison?
options: People who stutter versus controls
Children with DLD versus typically developing children
People with Parkinson's disease versus controls
Children at risk of later reading difficulty versus controls
questions.explanation: The 88% result belongs to a specific example and should not be generalized automatically.

questions.question: What Parkinson's voice-detection range is reported in the notes?
options: Roughly 85–90%
Exactly 100%
Exactly 50%
Roughly 20–25%
questions.explanation: This is the range reported by the notes, rather than an independently updated estimate.

questions.question: What benefit did the predictive multimodal AAC example report?
options: About 30% higher diagnostic accuracy
About 30% fewer clinicians needed for all care
About 30% better independent speech accuracy
About 30% less message construction time
questions.explanation: The example concerns message construction time in a particular framework.

questions.question: The Lexiland example reports which sensitivity and specificity?
options: 90% sensitivity and 76% specificity
100% sensitivity and 100% specificity
76% sensitivity and 90% specificity
50% sensitivity and 50% specificity
questions.explanation: The notes use these values to illustrate screening and triage trade-offs.

questions.question: What did improvement on untreated /r/ words illustrate in the remote-practice example?
options: Generalization beyond practiced items
Memorization limited to the trained word list
Transfer from screening directly to diagnosis
Evidence that clinician feedback is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Transfer to untreated words suggests learning beyond the exact practiced examples.

questions.question: Before applying a promising published tool locally, what matters most?
options: Only the strongest overall accuracy reported by the developers
Only validation on the original training population
Only whether its output matches clinical expectations in one case
Validation for similar ages, languages, dialects and disorders
questions.explanation: Early studies often use specific datasets that may differ from local patients.

questions.question: Why can an AI system reproduce population bias?
options: Its numerical design automatically removes social inequalities
It learns patterns from unrepresentative data
Only deliberate discriminatory instructions can create bias
A large dataset guarantees equal subgroup representation
questions.explanation: Who is included in training affects who benefits and who may be harmed.

questions.question: An ASR system works well on standard speech but poorly on a regional dialect. What should be investigated?
options: Dialect representation and subgroup error rates
Only the pooled accuracy across all dialects
Only transcription speed on standard speech
Only the recognizer's average confidence score
questions.explanation: Aggregate scores can conceal unequal performance across dialects.

questions.question: Why can adult-trained ASR fail on children's speech?
options: Adult-trained models automatically normalize all developmental differences
Children's speech needs only a larger test set without retraining
Age-related speech characteristics may be underrepresented
Any error on children's speech proves a language disorder
questions.explanation: A mismatch between training and use populations can reduce performance.

questions.question: What is the concern about geographically concentrated clinical datasets?
options: Large datasets from a few places automatically represent every language
Geographic concentration makes subgroup testing unnecessary
A shared medical label guarantees identical local conditions
Performance may not generalize to other settings
questions.explanation: The notes highlight concentration in the US and China as a generalizability concern.

questions.question: A tool trained on monolingual English-speaking children is used with bilingual children. What is the central risk?
options: Guaranteed transfer because both groups include some English
Linguistic and cultural mismatch
A need to remove the child's other language from assessment
Evidence that bilingualism itself is a disorder
questions.explanation: Training context should be compared with the intended population.

questions.question: Why did using healthcare cost as a proxy for health need create bias in the notes' example?
options: Spending and health need are interchangeable measures
A cost target guarantees equal access to referrals
Spending can reflect unequal access rather than actual need
Removing race as an input prevents all proxy bias
questions.explanation: A convenient target may encode existing inequalities.

questions.question: Which combination is recommended to mitigate bias?
options: A larger dataset, overall accuracy and no subgroup reporting
Removing demographic variables and assuming fairness
Representative data, subgroup audits and community involvement
Using the same threshold everywhere without auditing its effects
questions.explanation: Technical auditing and participation by affected communities complement each other.

questions.question: Why are voice recordings a privacy concern even after a name is removed?
options: Removing names always makes raw voice data anonymous
Only written transcripts can identify a person
A pseudonymous filename prevents all re-identification
The voice itself may help reveal identity
questions.explanation: Voice and language data can contain identifying and sensitive information.

questions.question: What does data minimization mean?
options: Share only data needed for the task
Share the complete history to avoid every possible omission
Remove identifiers but retain all other data regardless of need
Retain all recordings because they might be useful later
questions.explanation: The minimum necessary data reduces unnecessary exposure.

questions.question: Which description best follows the notes' de-identification example?
options: School, parent phone and full name
Child A, age 5;2
National ID and appointment number
Full name, birth date and address
questions.explanation: The notes model a pseudonymous case with clinically relevant age information.

questions.question: What should happen before AI-assisted recording or transcription?
options: Obtain informed consent using an approved workflow
Record first and obtain consent only if the output is useful
Treat attendance at therapy as consent for every external AI use
Use a public tool before asking about institutional approval
questions.explanation: Clients and caregivers should understand how AI is used.

questions.question: Which tool choice follows the notes' privacy guidance?
options: Any tool that states it uses encryption, without institutional review
A personal account chosen for convenience alone
A public tool after removing only the client's first name
An institution-approved tool with secure storage
questions.explanation: Approval, security and institutional policy matter when handling clinical information.

questions.question: What role should children and neurodivergent clients have in data use?
options: Participation only after all data decisions are finalized
Responsibility for verifying the vendor's training process
Automatic exclusion from decisions to avoid burdening them
A meaningful voice in decisions affecting them
questions.explanation: Autonomy includes involving affected people appropriately.

questions.question: How should a learner interpret the notes' discussion of HIPAA?
options: As a substitute for local policy
As permission to share de-identified audio publicly
As a US framework whose applicability depends on context
As a universal law applying identically everywhere
questions.explanation: The notes explicitly caution against assuming universal applicability.

questions.question: If no AI-specific rule clearly fits a setting, what do the notes recommend?
options: Ignore professional obligations
Follow applicable local data rules and institutional policy
Treat the absence of an AI law as unrestricted permission
Follow only a vendor's advertising
questions.explanation: Existing privacy and professional duties remain relevant.

questions.question: Which WHO principle supports meaningful patient choice?
options: Transparency and explainability
Responsibility and accountability
Responsive and sustainable AI
Protect autonomy
questions.explanation: The notes list autonomy among the six WHO principles.

questions.question: Which WHO principle addresses understandable AI use?
options: Inclusiveness and equity
Autonomy alone
Responsiveness and sustainability
Transparency, explainability and intelligibility
questions.explanation: Users should be able to understand relevant aspects of system operation and output.

questions.question: Which WHO principle concerns unequal access and unfair performance?
options: Inclusiveness and equity
Transparency alone
Environmental sustainability alone
Accountability alone
questions.explanation: Fair access and performance are ethical concerns, not just technical details.

questions.question: Who remains accountable for care decisions when AI is used?
options: Only the patient
Only the software vendor
The clinician
The algorithm itself
questions.explanation: Using a tool does not transfer professional responsibility to it.

questions.question: Why does sustainability appear in AI ethics?
options: Large models always use fewer resources than small ones
A clinically useful system has no environmental impact
Large models can have energy and carbon costs
Sustainability concerns only the lifetime of a device
questions.explanation: The notes include responsive and sustainable AI among the ethical principles.

questions.question: Which description best characterizes a trustworthy AI tool?
options: High overall accuracy without subgroup or privacy checks
Valid, safe, secure, fair and privacy-protecting
Fluent output combined with a persuasive explanation
Fast output and a high training-set score
questions.explanation: Trustworthiness involves several dimensions beyond apparent accuracy.

questions.question: Which evidence most strongly supports clinical trust?
options: Representative validation with subgroup results and intended-use limits
Repeatedly optimized performance on the same test set
High accuracy on training examples alone
A vendor demonstration using selected successful cases
questions.explanation: Independent relevant evaluation is stronger than marketing or training performance.

questions.question: What is an AI hallucination?
options: A false negative from a clinical screener only
Confidently stated content that is false or unsupported
An explicitly acknowledged uncertainty
A correct statement expressed with low confidence
questions.explanation: Hallucination can include invented facts, references or source details.

questions.question: Which output is a warning sign of hallucination?
options: A clear marker that the transcript did not state a detail
A highly specific statistic without a traceable source
A specific finding linked to a verified original source
A calculation shown from the provided trial counts
questions.explanation: Specificity and fluency do not supply evidence.

questions.question: An AI supplies a journal citation that cannot be located. What should the clinician do?
options: Keep it if its title matches the clinical topic
Verify independently and remove or correct it if unsupported
Ask the same model to repeat it and treat repetition as verification
Assume a correctly formatted citation must exist
questions.explanation: References must be checked against real sources.

questions.question: Why can a persuasive explanation be unsafe?
options: It may raise trust without being accurate or checkable
Any explanation directly exposes the model's true internal process
Clinical plausibility proves the explanation is causally faithful
A longer explanation removes the need for source checking
questions.explanation: Explainability should enable verification, rather than simply sound convincing.

questions.question: What should a pilot audit compare before wider clinical use?
options: Only pooled accuracy without subgroup breakdown
Only agreement with one clinician in a selected successful case
Performance across relevant subgroups
Only speed relative to manual work
questions.explanation: Pilots can expose age, language or dialect performance differences.

questions.question: Should AI alone decide whether a child qualifies for services?
options: Yes, if a single accuracy figure is high
Yes, if the tool is free
No, eligibility needs appropriate clinical judgment
Yes, if the text is confident
questions.explanation: The notes warn against using AI output alone to withhold services or determine eligibility.

questions.question: What is automation bias?
options: A guaranteed reduction in error
Overreliance on automated output
A preference for handwritten notes
A balanced independent appraisal
questions.explanation: Automation bias occurs when users defer too readily to a system.

questions.question: In the appraisal routine, what does the Source check ask?
options: Does the output fit the clinician's preferred writing style?
Does the model give the same answer twice?
Does the answer sound professionally worded?
Can every fact and citation be verified?
questions.explanation: Source checking tests whether claims are traceable.

questions.question: What does the Accuracy check compare?
options: AI output with observations and client data
AI output with the model's own confidence alone
AI output with a generic example from another patient
AI output with the vendor's accuracy claim alone
questions.explanation: Clinical data provide a necessary basis for checking an output.

questions.question: What does the Bias check examine?
options: Possible errors linked to language, dialect or culture
Only the model's overall published accuracy
Only whether race is an explicit input
Only whether the same threshold is used for everyone
questions.explanation: A polished output may still be inappropriate for a particular population.

questions.question: What does the Scope check ask?
options: Is AI making judgments reserved for the clinician?
Whether the output is longer than the original transcript
Whether the draft follows the requested table format
Whether the tool predicts a label with high confidence
questions.explanation: Diagnosis and prognosis require professional clinical judgment.

questions.question: What does the Privacy check ask?
options: Whether the answer includes a statement about confidentiality
Whether the clinician removed only the client's first name
Whether all generated text uses clinical terminology
Was identifiable information kept out?
questions.explanation: Privacy must be checked throughout the workflow.

questions.question: What does the Usefulness check examine?
options: Whether output improves care or saves meaningful time
Whether it produces more text than a manual note
Whether it matches the vendor's demonstration
Whether it eliminates every need for review
questions.explanation: A tool should add practical value after review costs are considered.

questions.question: What should happen if an appraisal step is unresolved?
options: Assume the next model version will fix it
Ignore the uncertain section
Correct or discard the output before use
Sign it immediately
questions.explanation: Uncertainty should trigger verification or rejection of the draft.

questions.question: A system misses a child who truly has a difficulty. What is this error?
options: True positive
True negative
False negative
False positive
questions.explanation: A false negative is an affected case incorrectly classified as negative.

questions.question: A system flags a child who does not have the difficulty. What is this error?
options: True positive
False positive
False negative
True negative
questions.explanation: A false positive is a positive prediction for an unaffected case.

questions.question: A tool's reported accuracy falls when used in a new dialect group. What concept is most relevant?
options: Perfect calibration
Poor generalizability
Guaranteed validity
Improved representativeness
questions.explanation: Performance in the development population may not transfer to a different population.

questions.question: Which question most directly addresses task clarity?
options: What data was it trained on?
What is the AI actually doing?
How accurate and validated is it?
Where does the SLP remain responsible?
questions.explanation: The slide deck asks users to clarify the actual computational task before trusting results.

questions.question: Why does a precise prompt generally reduce rework?
options: It makes the model's knowledge clinically validated
It prevents hallucinations without source checking
It replaces the need for developmentally appropriate review
It states the intended task and constraints clearly
questions.explanation: Specific instructions make the draft more likely to match the user's needs.

questions.question: Which set lists the six prompt components in the notes?
options: Role, task, context, format, constraints, examples
Name, address, diagnosis, password, payment, signature
Accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, recall, precision
Training, testing, deployment, billing, consent, audit
questions.explanation: The six components structure what the model should produce and how.

questions.question: What does the Role component specify?
options: The perspective the AI should adopt
The requested output structure
The specific activity to create
The de-identified details of the case
questions.explanation: A role frames the desired style and professional perspective without granting actual expertise.

questions.question: Which instruction states a Task?
options: Avoid identifying information
Act as a paediatric SLP
Create a home-practice activity
Use a three-column table
questions.explanation: The task names the output or action requested.

questions.question: Which information belongs in Context?
options: The requested number of table columns
The desired professional perspective alone
De-identified age, language background and relevant needs
The maximum activity duration alone
questions.explanation: Context makes material appropriate to the case while protecting identity.

questions.question: Which instruction specifies Format?
options: Present ten words and three steps in a table
Act as an SLP
Work with a five-year-old
Avoid diagnosis
questions.explanation: Format tells the system how to organize the answer.

questions.question: Which is a prompt Constraint?
options: Use caregiver-friendly language and no diagnosis
Act as a paediatric speech-language pathologist
Create a home-practice activity
Use a table with ten target words
questions.explanation: Constraints set limits on the output.

questions.question: What is zero-shot prompting?
options: Giving the task without examples
Providing one worked example
Providing three worked examples
Repeating an answer until it sounds correct
questions.explanation: Zero-shot means no demonstration examples are included.

questions.question: What is few-shot prompting in the notes?
options: Providing no demonstration examples
Providing a small number of examples, such as one to three
Requesting several outputs without examples
Retraining a model on a complete dataset
questions.explanation: Examples help communicate the requested style or response pattern.

questions.question: What should a speech-sound prompt specify beyond the sound itself?
options: Only how many times the sound occurs across the whole list
Its target position, such as initial /s/
Only the maximum number of words in the response
Only the type of table to use
questions.explanation: Target position helps align word choices with the intended practice goal.

questions.question: Why include developmental level as well as age?
options: Chronological age automatically predicts every language skill
Developmental level determines whether consent is necessary
To match vocabulary and activity demands to the child
A stated age guarantees suitable vocabulary without checking
questions.explanation: Age alone may not capture the level of support or language complexity needed.

questions.question: What should linguistic context include?
options: Languages, dialect and familiar cultural references
Only the language preferred by the model
Only the language of the original textbook
Only the clinician's professional terminology
questions.explanation: Materials should fit the child's actual language environment.

questions.question: Why specify the audience and reading level?
options: Technical language is equally useful for all readers
Reading level determines whether statements are true
An audience label makes citation checking unnecessary
A caregiver may need different wording from a clinician
questions.explanation: The same information can require different presentation for different readers.

questions.question: Which prompt is more clinically usable?
options: Write anything long
Create a guaranteed cure
Make something about speech
Create a 15-minute initial /s/ activity with ten target words and caregiver tips
questions.explanation: The specific prompt states target, duration, quantity and audience.

questions.question: A draft uses unfamiliar cultural objects. What is a useful refinement?
options: Add more diagnostic claims
Insert the child's full name
Accept them because the grammar is correct
Replace them with familiar objects from the child's setting
questions.explanation: Follow-up prompts can improve contextual fit.

questions.question: What should be verified in generated target words?
options: Only that the requested number of words is present
Only that each item is a familiar noun
That the words are real and contain the intended target
Only that each word has the same syllable count
questions.explanation: A neat format does not ensure accurate phonological targeting.

questions.question: What is the best status for a first AI-generated activity?
options: A draft requiring refinement and verification
A validated intervention ready for use without checking
A clinical recommendation equivalent to a full assessment
A final activity once it matches the requested format
questions.explanation: The notes advise an iterative process followed by checking.

questions.question: What privacy rule applies during follow-up prompting?
options: Share the full record after one revision
Keep identifying details out at every step
Add identifiers if the draft seems generic
Only the first prompt needs de-identification
questions.explanation: Privacy duties continue through the entire conversation.

questions.question: A prompt says 'act as an expert.' What does this guarantee?
options: No guarantee of factual or clinical correctness
Validated clinical reasoning
Accurate citations in every answer
Institutional approval
questions.explanation: Role wording guides generation but does not verify the output.

questions.question: Which instruction helps prevent invented details in a draft?
options: Use only supplied information and mark what is missing
Infer typical observations where the transcript is incomplete
Use a polished narrative without missing-data markers
Make uncertain details sound like established observations
questions.explanation: Clear constraints reduce unsupported additions, but checking is still required.

questions.question: What is the first step in the notes' documentation workflow?
options: De-identify a recording obtained without prior consent
Generate a SOAP draft before reviewing recording permissions
Record or transcribe with consent using an approved tool
Sign the draft before comparing it with the transcript
questions.explanation: Consent and an approved process precede AI-assisted drafting.

questions.question: What should happen to a transcript before it is supplied to an LLM?
options: Remove only the client's first name and retain all other identifiers
Insert a likely diagnosis to improve the model's context
Merge prompted and independent successes to simplify the input
De-identify it
questions.explanation: De-identification reduces exposure of identifying information.

questions.question: How should missing information be handled in a SOAP draft?
options: Infer the most likely value from similar patients
Treat an omitted detail as a normal finding
Use a typical value without labeling it as an assumption
Mark it as [NOT STATED]
questions.explanation: Explicit missing-data markers preserve the boundary between evidence and inference.

questions.question: What should happen before a clinician signs an AI-assisted note?
options: Check grammar and formatting without checking facts
Accept the note if it has all four SOAP headings
Ask the model to confirm its own accuracy
Check and correct it against the transcript and observations
questions.explanation: The clinician remains responsible for the final signed record.

questions.question: Which description best fits the LLM's documentation role?
options: A drafting scribe under clinician review
The treating clinician
The owner of the care plan
The final diagnostic authority
questions.explanation: The notes explicitly place clinical responsibility with the clinician.

questions.question: What belongs in Subjective?
options: Measurable trial counts and prompt levels
Clinical interpretation of progress
Client or caregiver report
Next goals and home-practice frequency
questions.explanation: Subjective information includes reported experience, confirmed by the clinician.

questions.question: What belongs in Objective?
options: Caregiver descriptions of behavior at home
The clinician's interpretation of progress
Planned treatment frequency and future targets
Measurable trials, accuracy and prompt levels
questions.explanation: Objective data should be traceable to what was measured or observed.

questions.question: What belongs in Assessment?
options: The caregiver's reported concerns
Raw counts with no interpretation
Clinical interpretation of progress
The next appointment schedule alone
questions.explanation: The clinician writes or approves interpretation.

questions.question: What belongs in Plan?
options: Only the client's report of the previous week
Next goals, frequency and home practice
Only the measured success rate from the session
Only the interpretation of the present results
questions.explanation: Plans concern subsequent care and require clinician approval.

questions.question: Which section should contain 'caregiver reports difficulty practicing at home'?
options: Objective
Assessment
Plan
Subjective
questions.explanation: This is reported experience rather than a counted performance measure.

questions.question: Which section should contain 'two independent correct responses in six trials'?
options: Subjective
Objective
Assessment
Plan
questions.explanation: Trial counts are measurable session data.

questions.question: What does I+ mean in the notes' coding scheme?
options: Correct after prompting
No response
Correct independently
Incorrect response

General intelligence depends only on the number of trained models

questions.explanation: Specificity is true negatives divided by all genuinely unaffected cases: 76/100.

questions.question: A tool flags 40 children, of whom 30 truly have the difficulty. What is precision?
questions.explanation: Precision is true positives divided by all flagged cases: 30/40.

questions.question: A classifier is correct for 85 of 100 evaluated cases. What is accuracy?
questions.explanation: Accuracy uses all correct classifications over all evaluated cases.

questions.question: A screener misses 5 of 20 genuinely affected children. What is sensitivity?
questions.explanation: There are 15 true positives, so sensitivity is 15/20.

questions.question: A six-trial record contains 3 I+, 1 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR. What is independent accuracy?
questions.explanation: Independent accuracy is 3/6. Prompted successes are excluded from its numerator.

questions.question: For 3 I+, 1 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is accuracy with support?
options: Approximately 67%
questions.explanation: All four correct responses are counted over six trials.

questions.question: For 3 I+, 1 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is prompt dependence?
questions.explanation: Prompt dependence is 1/(3+1), which is 25%.

questions.question: A child has no correct responses. How should P+ divided by (I+ + P+) be handled?
options: Invent a correct response
Report it as undefined rather than divide by zero
Report 50% automatically
Report 100% automatically
questions.explanation: With no correct trials the denominator is zero, so that ratio cannot be calculated.

questions.question: A report gives overall accuracy but no language-group breakdown. What is the best next request?
options: A promise of perfect performance
A longer advertising description
Subgroup performance and relevant validation details
Only the model's logo
questions.explanation: Overall results may conceal poorer performance in a language group.

questions.question: An LLM combines 2 I+ and 2 P+ as four independent successes. What should the reviewer correct?
options: Remove every trial count
Keep the total as independent accuracy
Change the child's age
Separate independent from prompted responses and recalculate
questions.explanation: The mistake inflates independent skill by merging response categories.

questions.question: A generated note includes a client name that was missed during de-identification. What is the next step?
options: Add the client's address for consistency
Ignore it if the diagnosis is correct
Remove the identifier and follow the approved privacy process
Continue because only the final note matters
questions.explanation: Privacy checking includes identifiers in both inputs and drafts.

questions.question: A parent asks whether a positive AI screen proves DLD. What is the appropriate explanation?
options: It guarantees the same result in every language
It means therapy can be prescribed without review
It is a conclusive diagnosis
It indicates risk and needs full assessment
questions.explanation: The notes distinguish screening from diagnosis.

questions.question: An activity lists words lacking the requested initial /s/. What should happen?
options: Remove all instructions and keep the words
Accept it because the table is attractive
Correct the word list before use
Change the child's target to match the list
questions.explanation: Generated materials must be checked for the actual target sound and position.

questions.question: A user sets a paediatric SLP role but omits age, target and audience. What is the best improvement?
options: Use only more enthusiastic language
Add the client's complete medical record
Assume the model knows the case
Add de-identified context and precise output requirements
questions.explanation: Role alone does not communicate the relevant task details.

questions.question: Which support sequence is stated in the lecture notes?
options: Model, physical, verbal, independent, visual
Verbal, physical, independent, model, visual
Physical, independent, model, verbal, gestural
Independent, verbal, model, gestural/visual, physical
questions.explanation: This reproduces the hierarchy as presented in the supplied notes.

questions.question: What administrative benefit do the notes describe?
options: Eliminating all review duties
Removing consent requirements
Guaranteeing every assessment score
Reducing time spent drafting notes and reports
questions.explanation: Speech-to-text and summarization may reduce documentation burden when properly reviewed.

questions.question: What approximate publication growth rate is reported in the notes?
options: 100% per month
1% per decade
16.5% per year
0% per year
questions.explanation: This is the figure reported in the notes, not an independently updated literature estimate.

questions.question: What average waiting-list figure is cited in the notes?
options: Exactly one day
Around eight years
Around eight months
Exactly one week
questions.explanation: The notes use this reported figure to motivate early-access opportunities.

questions.question: What can multimodal data help identify for personalization?
options: A reason to ignore clinical history
A guaranteed universal treatment
The child's identity without consent
Which language subsystems drive a child's difficulty
questions.explanation: The notes connect different data sources with tailored targets and intensity.

questions.question: When six trials include no independent successes and three prompted successes, what is independent accuracy?
options: Undefined
questions.explanation: The denominator is six, so zero independent successes gives 0/6 rather than an undefined ratio.

questions.question: Which system defeated Garry Kasparov in 1997?
options: EMI
Metacat
IBM Deep Blue
Cyc
questions.explanation: The prologue uses computer chess to question assumptions about intelligence.

questions.question: Why did Deep Blue challenge Hofstadter's earlier expectation?
options: It showed that every computer had emotions
It learned every human language
Narrow chess mastery did not require broad general intelligence
It needed no specialized engineering
questions.explanation: The example separates success in chess from general humanlike ability.

questions.question: What surprised listeners in the EMI comparison described in the prologue?
options: They could mistake generated music for a human composer's work
Every listener identified every piece correctly
The program could not produce sound
The audience had no musical experience
questions.explanation: The incident raised questions about style imitation and perceived creativity.

questions.question: What particularly disturbed Hofstadter in the prologue?
options: The possibility that valued human creativity could be matched by superficial mechanisms
Only the length of music recordings
A proven inability of AI to generate anything
Only the price of computers
questions.explanation: His concern extended beyond physical danger to the meaning of human capacities.

questions.question: What is the book's stated aim?
options: Guarantee a date for general intelligence
Supply clinical treatment protocols
Provide a complete programming manual for all AI
Examine how selected AI methods work, succeed and fail
questions.explanation: Mitchell presents a critical exploration rather than a complete history or technical manual.
